item.title: Battle of the Frontiers: The Chaotic First Two Weeks of World War I
item.description: WWI's opening two weeks saw the Battle of the Frontiers when German armies advanced through Belgium into France and French armies advanced into German-held Alsace. Both sides wanted the major battles to be in the enemy's territory and in achieving this objective, Germany won.

item.title: Mesopotamian Art and Architecture: The Birth of Art and Architecture in the Ancient World
item.description: Mesopotamian monumental architecture is epitomized by the ziggurat, but the Sumerians were also responsible for the first large-scale palaces and temples, as well as urban planning, the arch, canals and aqueducts, landscaped gardens, and architectural ornamentation. These early innovations would become more refined in the region through succeeding periods and influence the works of other cultures in the Near East and Mediterranean regions.

item.title: Anne Hutchinson: Spiritual Visionary and Champion of Faith
item.description: Anne Hutchinson is regarded as a "founding mother" and an impressive figure of Colonial America who asserted her personal dignity and rights in a time when women were given no voice to do so. She was a religious reformer, Puritan dissident, midwife, and alleged prophetess whose beliefs and influence brought her into conflict with the magistrates of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, especially its governor, John Winthrop, in 1636-1638. item.title: Mesopotamian Inventions: Creating the Future
item.description: Among the Mesopotamians' most important inventions was writing, through the system they developed known as cuneiform, which has preserved the beliefs, history, and culture of the region that would significantly influence later civilizations in every respect. item.title: First Battle of the Marne: How Paris was Saved in World War I
item.description: Hopes of a quick German victory over France were dashed at the Battle of the Marne. The Allies, bruised and bashed, had survived the first chaotic weeks of the war. Somehow, Germany's great push had been stopped in what became known as the ‘Miracle of the Marne'. Two million men had fought, and one quarter of them had already become casualties of a war only six weeks old.

item.title: Trade in Ancient Mesopotamia: How Commerce Encouraged Civilization
item.description: Trade began in Mesopotamia for the same reason it did anywhere else – need. The Mesopotamians had a surplus of grain, clay, and reeds (among other assets) that they could offer in return for resources they lacked, such as precious metals, minerals, and wood from other regions. The development of long-distance trade during the Ubaid and Uruk periods led to the invention of writing in the form of cuneiform script by circa 3500 BCE so that merchants could communicate with clients in foreign regions

item.title: Marcus Junius Brutus: Rome's Most Notorious Traitor
item.description: Marcus Junius Brutus is alternately remembered as a noble man who acted in opposition to tyranny or as one of the most notorious traitors in history. Said to have been descended from the semi-legendary founder of the Roman Republic, Brutus came to oppose the autocratic behavior shown by Caesar after the latter became dictator. Brutus and the other conspirators decided to attack Caesar at a Senate meeting, which would be held at the Senate House in the Portico of Pompey on the Ides of March.

item.title: The Trial of Anne Hutchinson: Silencing Dissent in Colonial America
item.description: Anne Hutchinson was brought to trial by John Winthrop and the other magistrates of the Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1637 for spreading "erroneous opinions" regarding religious belief and practice. item.title: Battle of Passchendaele: Haig's Folly in the Mud of Flanders
item.description: The Third Battle of Ypres was widely seen as an Allied failure. Strictly speaking, Haig had won the battle, but the gains were minimal and the costs high. The British and British Empire forces had overall suffered between 250,000 and 275,000 casualties (including 70,000 killed) in three months of fighting for no strategic gain. item.title: Scribes in Ancient Mesopotamia: The Beginning of History
item.description: Scribes in Mesopotamia were initially tasked with recording transactions in trade and keeping records. Eventually, they became an integral part of everyday life and were involved in trade, royal correspondence, record-keeping at the temple complex, military matters, long-distance correspondence, construction of new buildings, and agricultural concerns, among many other tasks. They also composed original compositions and, essentially, created what we know as history.
